"We've seen examples where three or four or five papers with the exact same proof of the exact same theorem have come out within a couple days of each other, which is clearly some situation where someone's playing the slot machine."

"It's not obvious that this problem goes away as the models get better. Maybe it does, but maybe it doesn't."

"A lot of progress in mathematics comes from letting a thousand different flowers bloom and people pursue their own curiosity, and then the boundaries of knowledge expand in some fairly uniform way... and then opportunistically you suddenly get applications or answers to old questions."

"It's not clear to me that if we subordinate mathematical exploration to what the models want to pursue... [whether] what you're getting is one mathematician duplicated 1,000 times, or a million different mathematicians doing a million different things."

The models are good at a narrower slice of math than the headlines suggest. They grind long computations, pull technical ideas from more papers than any human could read, and apply every known technique better than almost anyone.

Social Security hits the wall in 2032.

When the trust fund runs dry, benefits get cut 22% automatically, for every retiree at once. The program already spends more than it collects, and the shortfall widens to nearly 7% of every taxable paycheck by the 2080s.

There are 3 ways out: cut benefits, hike the 12.4% payroll tax, or fund the gap from the general budget. Washington picks the last one, because a 22% cut to nearly 70 million voters ends careers. That means borrowing the difference, more Treasury supply stacked on the deficit that already has long yields climbing.

Either retirees take the cut in 2032, or the bond market pays for the delay.

It's not a plan to "seize" deposits.

It's a capital markets project that will make it easier for  banks to pool loans and sell them as securities, transferring risk and thus freeing regulatory capital for even more lending.
